reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: Usually caused by heterozygous, often de novo, variants in SLC2A1 encoding the glucose transporter GLUT1, with dominant inheritance
GLUT1 mediates glucose transport across the blood-brain barrier, so its deficiency produces a state of chronic cerebral energy shortage
The classic phenotype combines early-onset drug-resistant epilepsy, acquired microcephaly, developmental delay and a complex movement disorder
A hallmark biochemical finding is low cerebrospinal fluid glucose (hypoglycorrhachia) with a low CSF-to-blood glucose ratio in the presence of normal blood glucose
Paroxysmal exercise-induced dyskinesia and symptoms that worsen with fasting and improve after meals are characteristic clues
The ketogenic diet is the treatment of choice because ketone bodies provide an alternative cerebral fuel that bypasses the transporter defect
Phenotypes range from severe classic disease to milder paroxysmal movement disorders or absence epilepsy without major cognitive impairment
A lumbar puncture should be performed after a period of fasting and before glucose administration to avoid a falsely normal ratio
reference.pathophysiology: GLUT1 deficiency syndrome results from reduced function of the GLUT1 glucose transporter, which is responsible for moving glucose across the blood-brain barrier and into astrocytes and other cells. Because the brain depends heavily on glucose as its principal fuel, impaired transport causes a chronic shortfall of energy substrate within the central nervous system despite normal systemic glucose. This cerebral energy deficiency underlies the seizures, movement disorder and impaired brain growth. Ketone bodies enter the brain via monocarboxylate transporters independent of GLUT1, which is why a ketogenic diet can supply alternative fuel and improve symptoms.
additionalDifferentials: Mitochondrial disorders with movement disorder and seizures
additionalInvestigations: Lumbar puncture measuring CSF glucose with a paired fasting blood glucose to calculate the ratio
CSF lactate, which is typically low or low-normal
Electroencephalography, sometimes showing improvement after a meal
Brain MRI, often normal but useful to exclude alternatives
Red-cell glucose uptake studies where available
redFlags: Drug-resistant seizures beginning in infancy with developmental slowing
Symptoms clearly worsening with fasting or exertion
Progressive movement disorder with ataxia and dystonia
reference.prognosis: Seizures and movement symptoms often respond well to a ketogenic diet, and early dietary treatment can improve neurological function, but many patients retain some degree of cognitive and motor impairment. Prognosis is generally better in milder phenotypes and with early initiation of ketogenic therapy.
pitfalls: Performing the lumbar puncture after glucose administration or a meal, masking hypoglycorrhachia
Attributing drug-resistant epilepsy to other causes and missing a treatable diagnosis
Not recognising fasting- and exercise-related symptom fluctuation
Overlooking milder paroxysmal movement or absence-epilepsy phenotypes
references: Scriver's Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease
management: Establish a ketogenic diet as the treatment of choice, providing ketones that cross the blood-brain barrier independently of GLUT1 to relieve the chronic cerebral energy deficit
Avoid GLUT1 inhibitors and ketosis-lowering agents, notably caffeine and methylxanthines, and prevent prolonged fasting
Add antiseizure medication for seizures not fully controlled by diet, favouring agents that do not impair ketosis
Provide symptomatic management of the movement disorder, including ataxia, dystonia and paroxysmal exercise-induced dyskinesia, with physiotherapy and rehabilitation
Monitor ketosis, growth, lipids, bone health and for renal calculi while on the ketogenic diet
Coordinate multidisciplinary care across metabolic medicine, neurology, dietetics and developmental services
Offer genetic counselling, noting frequent de novo dominant SLC2A1 variants, with testing of parents where relevant
